summary: The proposal is well-structured with a clear problem statement, well-defined objectives, and a realistic iteration-based schedule, and no structural, figure, or schedule issues were identified. The primary weakness is the pervasive use of first-person 'I' (approximately 24 instances), which directly violates the stated style guidelines and requires a systematic rewrite. Secondary issues include inconsistent terminology across sections, a book reference reduced to a store-page URL, and a slightly incomplete AI transparency statement—all straightforward fixes that will bring the proposal to submission-ready quality.

findings.title: Excessive use of first-person 'I' throughout the proposal
findings.description: The guidelines state: "Avoid 'one,' 'I,' and 'our.' Use 'we' sparingly, only for the thesis approach." The student uses 'I' approximately 20 times in the main body (Abstract, Objective sections, Schedule) and 4 additional times in the AI Transparency Statement. The text should be restructured to use 'we' (sparingly, for the thesis approach) or to omit the subject where the actor is clear from context. For example, 'I develop a self-service platform' becomes 'We develop a self-service platform' or 'This thesis develops a self-service platform'; 'I reach this objective when…' becomes 'This objective is reached when…' or 'We reach this objective when…'. The Schedule bullets can drop the subject entirely: 'I deliver the Keycloak realm' → 'Deliver the Keycloak realm' or 'We deliver the Keycloak realm.'

findings.title: Inconsistent terminology for the same concepts throughout the proposal
findings.description: Three pairs of terms are used inconsistently for the same concepts. (1) 'Administrative privileges' (Abstract, Objective) vs. 'administrative rights' (Introduction, Problem) for the elevated system permissions maintainers should not hold. (2) 'Compute hosts' (Abstract, Problem) vs. 'Linux hosts' (Introduction, Figure 3 caption, Objective) for the same group of machines. (3) 'Drift check' (Section 4.2, twice) vs. 'drift report' (Schedule, Iteration 5) for the same deliverable. Pick one term per concept and use it consistently throughout. If 'drift check' and 'drift report' are genuinely different (process vs. output), make that distinction explicit.

findings.title: Scientific book cited as a store-URL footnote instead of a proper bibliography entry
findings.description: The book by Bruegge and Dutoit (Object-Oriented Software Engineering Using UML, Patterns, and Java) is referenced in the body text as footnote 3, which contains only a URL to the Pearson store page. As a scientific/academic book, it is an eligible bibliography entry. A bare store-page URL does not provide standard bibliographic details (full title, publisher, edition, year, ISBN). The student should either move the reference into the Bibliography section with full publication details, or at minimum expand the footnote to include the proper bibliographic citation (authors, title, publisher, year, edition) rather than just a product-page URL.

findings.title: AI transparency statement lacks explicit 'correct and make sense' confirmation language
findings.description: The transparency statement confirms the author checked the AI-generated text, but it does not explicitly state the purpose of that checking in the required phrasing. The guidelines expect language similar to 'I have carefully checked all texts created with these tools to ensure that they are correct and make sense.' The student's sentence lists specific corrective actions (revised, verified, compiled, inspected) but omits the explicit confirmation that the checking was done to ensure correctness and coherence. Adding a clause such as 'to ensure that they are correct and make sense' would fully satisfy the requirement.

locations.section: Transparency in the Use of AI Tools
locations.quote: I carefully checked all AI-generated text, revised it where necessary, verified every citation against the original publication, and compiled and inspected every diagram.
